title: System Design Concepts Course and Interview Prep
description: A structured path through freeCodeCamp’s system design interview-prep video with Hayk Simonyan. Watch each chapter in the original YouTube video, then use the summary, quiz, and exercise to lock in the idea. The course surveys the core building blocks of scalable systems: architecture, CAP and service objectives, networking, APIs, caching, proxies, load balancing, and databases.

source.name: freeCodeCamp.org
source.creator: Hayk Simonyan
source.videoTitle: System Design Concepts Course and Interview Prep

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.summary: Hayk Simonyan frames this as a crash course on the system design interview concepts you need, covering scalability, reliability, data handling, and high-level architecture. He stresses that the interview is not mainly about writing code; interviewers want to see how you glue an entire large-scale system together.

quiz.question: What is a system design interview mainly trying to assess, according to this course’s framing?
choices: How quickly you can write production-ready code on a whiteboard
How you connect the parts of a large system, not how you write the implementation code
Whether you can memorize every AWS product name
How many sorting algorithms you can implement
quiz.explanation: The course describes the interview as being about gluing an entire system together rather than writing actual code.

quiz.question: Which trio does the course treat as central activities in system design?
choices: Compiling, linking, and deploying
Moving data, storing data, and transforming data
Marketing, billing, and support
Linting, formatting, and testing
quiz.explanation: Those three activities are the high-level lens used at the start of the course.

exercise.prompt: In two or three sentences, describe a product you know (for example a chat app or a shop) in terms of how it moves, stores, and transforms data.
exercise.hint: Moving might be a user request or a message between services; storing might be a database or object store; transforming might be creating a feed, a receipt, or an analytics aggregate.

lessons.title: Computer architecture

chapters.title: Computer Architecture (Disk Storage, RAM, Cache, CPU)

lessons.summary: Before designing distributed systems, the course reviews how a single computer actually runs code. Computers work in layers and, at the core, only understand binary bits. The lesson then walks the storage and compute hierarchy — disk, RAM, cache, and the CPU — so you have intuition for why some operations are cheap, why memory is scarce, and why caches exist.

quiz.question: In the usual storage hierarchy, which of these is typically the fastest but smallest?
choices: Hard disk or SSD storage
RAM
CPU cache
Magnetic tape backup
quiz.explanation: Cache sits closest to the CPU: it is small and expensive, but much faster than RAM or disk.

quiz.question: Why does this hardware review matter in a system design interview?
choices: Interviewers only hire people who can solder RAM
It explains why some operations are cheap or slow, and why we cache data closer to the processor or the user
It replaces the need to talk about databases
It proves that disk is always faster than memory
quiz.explanation: The point is performance intuition, not hardware assembly.

exercise.prompt: Order disk, RAM, and CPU cache from fastest to slowest, and write one sentence about why an application might keep a frequently used value in memory instead of reading it from disk every time.
exercise.hint: Fastest is cache, then RAM, then disk. Re-reading from disk on every request adds latency.

lessons.title: Production app architecture

chapters.title: Production App Architecture (CI/CD, Load Balancers, Logging & Monitoring)

lessons.summary: A production app is more than one process on a laptop. Hayk starts with a CI/CD pipeline (continuous integration and continuous deployment) so code can go from a repository through tests and onto production without manual steps, using tools such as Jenkins or GitHub Actions. He then places load balancers in front of the app and adds logging and monitoring so you can see what the system is doing once it is live.

quiz.question: Which CI/CD tools does this lesson mention as examples for automating deployment?
choices: Jenkins or GitHub Actions
Only Photoshop
Only FTP clients
Excel macros
quiz.explanation: Hayk names platforms such as Jenkins or GitHub Actions for automating the path from the repository through tests to production.

quiz.question: Besides a CI/CD pipeline, which supporting pieces appear in this high-level production architecture?
choices: Load balancers plus logging and monitoring
Only a single laptop process with no tests
A paper filing cabinet
A CSS preprocessor only
quiz.explanation: The production picture includes CI/CD, load balancing in front of the app, and logging and monitoring once it is live.

exercise.prompt: Sketch a simple production path for a web app: developer commit → CI/CD → running instances behind a load balancer, plus one place logs or metrics would be sent. Label each box.
exercise.hint: A typical path is repo → build/test pipeline → deploy to several app servers, with a load balancer in front and a log or metrics store on the side.

lessons.title: CAP, throughput, latency, SLOs and SLAs

chapters.title: Design Requirements (CAP Theorem, Throughput, Latency, SLOs and SLAs)

lessons.summary: The section opens with what makes a good design: scalability as the system grows with its users, maintainability so future developers can change it, and efficiency in how resources are used, plus planning for failure. It then covers the CAP theorem (you can fully guarantee only two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance), throughput versus latency, and the difference between SLOs (internal targets) and SLAs (external commitments).

quiz.question: What does the CAP theorem say you can fully guarantee at once in a distributed system?
choices: Consistency, availability, and partition tolerance, always all three
Only two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
Only throughput and latency
Only SLOs, never SLAs
quiz.explanation: When the network partitions, you usually have to trade between consistency and availability.

quiz.question: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
choices: They are two names for the same metric
Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how much work the system completes in a period
Throughput is only used for disks; latency is only used for networks
Latency measures availability; throughput measures consistency
quiz.explanation: A system can have high throughput and still feel slow to one user if latency is high.

quiz.question: How do SLOs and SLAs typically differ?
choices: SLOs are internal targets; SLAs are external commitments, often with consequences if missed
SLAs are only used by front-end teams; SLOs are only used by databases
An SLO is a legal contract; an SLA is a cache setting
They are identical terms
quiz.explanation: You set SLOs to run the service; an SLA is the promise you make to customers or partners.

exercise.prompt: Pick a system (for example a bank transfer API or a social feed). Write whether you would lean toward consistency or availability if the network partitions, and give one latency or throughput target you might set as an SLO.
exercise.hint: A bank usually favors consistency (correct balances) over always being available. A feed might accept slightly stale data to stay up. An SLO might be ‘p99 latency under 200 ms’ or ‘99.9% of requests succeed’.

lessons.title: TCP, UDP, DNS, and IP

chapters.title: Networking (TCP, UDP, DNS, IP Addresses & IP Headers)

lessons.summary: Networking basics cover how machines find each other and exchange packets. IP addresses identify hosts, and IP headers carry routing metadata. DNS maps human-readable names to addresses. TCP is a connection-oriented, reliable transport; UDP is a lighter, connectionless transport that does not guarantee delivery or order — a trade-off that shows up later in API and real-time protocol choices.

quiz.question: What is DNS used for?
choices: Compressing images before they are stored
Mapping a domain name to an IP address
Guaranteeing that UDP packets arrive in order
Encrypting a database at rest
quiz.explanation: DNS is the name system of the internet: example.com becomes an address a client can contact.

quiz.question: Which statement about TCP and UDP is accurate?
choices: UDP is always slower than TCP because it retries more often
TCP is connection-oriented and aims to deliver data reliably; UDP is lighter and does not guarantee delivery or order
TCP cannot be used for HTTP
UDP assigns IP addresses to hosts
quiz.explanation: TCP adds handshake, acknowledgements, and ordering. UDP skips that overhead.

exercise.prompt: For each of these, choose TCP or UDP and say why: a bank’s payment API, a live video call, and a DNS lookup (as typically designed).
exercise.hint: Payments usually want TCP’s reliability. Real-time media often uses UDP so a late packet can be dropped instead of stalling the stream. Classic DNS queries are often UDP.

lessons.title: Application layer protocols

chapters.title: Application Layer Protocols (HTTP, WebSockets, WebRTC, MQTT, etc)

lessons.summary: Once packets can move, applications still need a protocol for meaning. HTTP is called out as the most common application-layer protocol, the request/response model for the web and many APIs. The lesson also covers WebSockets for an open bidirectional channel, WebRTC for real-time audio and video, MQTT for lightweight publish/subscribe (often used in IoT), and mentions protocols such as SSH in the same survey.

quiz.question: When would WebSockets usually be a better fit than plain request/response HTTP?
choices: For a one-off download of a static image
When the client and server need an open, bidirectional channel for frequent updates
When you only need to send a single form submission
When you want to avoid all networking
quiz.explanation: Chat, live feeds, and similar apps often need the server to push data without a new HTTP request each time.

quiz.question: Which protocol is commonly associated with lightweight publish/subscribe messaging, including IoT devices?
choices: FTP
MQTT
SMTP only
CSS
quiz.explanation: MQTT is designed as a compact pub/sub protocol for constrained clients and unreliable networks.

exercise.prompt: Choose a protocol (HTTP, WebSockets, WebRTC, or MQTT) for: (1) a product catalog API, (2) an in-browser video call, and (3) thousands of sensors reporting temperature. Write one reason for each.
exercise.hint: Catalog: HTTP. Video call: WebRTC. Sensors: MQTT (or a similar pub/sub protocol).

modules.title: APIs, caches, proxies, and load balancers

lessons.title: API design
lessons.summary: This section starts from API basics and works toward practical habits for interfaces that other developers can use as a system grows: clear resource-oriented contracts, consistent naming and status codes, versioning so you can change a contract safely, and thinking about pagination, errors, and idempotency so retries do not corrupt data.

quiz.question: Why does API versioning matter in a production system?
choices: It lets you change a contract without immediately breaking existing clients
It makes DNS resolve faster
It replaces the need for authentication
It automatically shards your database
quiz.explanation: A versioned path or header gives old clients a stable API while new clients adopt the new one.

quiz.question: What does it mean for an API operation to be idempotent?
choices: It can never return an error
Repeating the same request has the same effect as doing it once
It must use UDP
It always creates a new record
quiz.explanation: Idempotency is important when networks retry. A well-designed PUT or a request with an idempotency key should not double-charge or double-create.

exercise.prompt: Design a tiny REST-style API for a library: list endpoints to list books, get one book, and borrow a book. Note one status code you would return on success and one on a client error, and say whether borrow should be idempotent if the client retries.
exercise.hint: Example: GET /books, GET /books/{id}, POST /books/{id}/borrow. 200 or 201 on success, 400 or 404 on client errors. Retries should not borrow the same copy twice.

lessons.title: Caching and CDNs
lessons.summary: Hayk motivates caching with a company hosting a website on a cloud server that is far from some users. A cache stores a computed or fetched result closer to the next reader, and a CDN is a geographically distributed cache so users hit a nearby edge instead of the origin. You also have to plan invalidation and what happens on a cache miss, because stale or missing data is the usual trade-off. Faster load times are treated as part of a better user experience.

quiz.question: What problem do caches and CDNs mainly try to improve?
choices: They replace the need for a database
They reduce latency and load on the origin by serving stored copies of data or content
They guarantee strong consistency across every region
They make CAP trade-offs disappear
quiz.explanation: A cache hit avoids a slower trip to the origin. A CDN does that from a location nearer the user.

quiz.question: What is a cache invalidation problem?
choices: Deciding when a stored copy is too old or must be replaced after the source changes
Converting HTTP to WebSockets
Assigning IP addresses to cache servers
Writing the first line of a unit test
quiz.explanation: If you never invalidate, users can see stale data. If you invalidate too aggressively, you lose the benefit of the cache.

exercise.prompt: For a news website’s article pages, say what you might cache at a CDN, what should probably not be cached for long, and one way you would expire or purge a page after an editor updates it.
exercise.hint: The rendered article and images are good CDN candidates. Personalized account widgets should stay short-lived or uncached. Use a short TTL, a cache key with a version, or a purge when the article is published.

lessons.title: Forward and reverse proxies
lessons.summary: Proxy servers act as an intermediary on the request path. A forward proxy sits in front of clients and can send their requests onward (for example for egress control or filtering). A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers: clients talk to the proxy, and it forwards to the right origin. Reverse proxies are often used for TLS termination, caching, routing, and shielding backends.

quiz.question: Where does a reverse proxy sit?
choices: In front of your servers, so clients send requests to the proxy rather than directly to each origin
Only on the user’s laptop, never in the data center
Between two database replicas only
Inside the CPU cache
quiz.explanation: Clients know the proxy’s address. The proxy chooses or protects the backend.

quiz.question: What is a typical job of a forward proxy?
choices: Sharding a database by user id
Acting on behalf of clients when they make outbound requests, for example to filter or control egress
Writing CI/CD pipelines
Replacing DNS entirely
quiz.explanation: Forward proxies represent the client side; reverse proxies represent the server side.

exercise.prompt: Draw or describe two tiny diagrams: a browser going through a forward proxy to the public internet, and many browsers going to a reverse proxy that forwards to three app servers. Label which proxy is which.
exercise.hint: Forward: clients → forward proxy → internet. Reverse: clients → reverse proxy → your app servers.

lessons.title: Load balancers
lessons.summary: Load balancers are described as perhaps the most popular use of proxy servers. They distribute incoming traffic across multiple instances so no single server is the only path, which improves availability and helps you scale horizontally. They often run health checks and stop sending traffic to sick nodes. A load balancer can itself become a single point of failure if you only run one.

quiz.question: What is the main job of a load balancer?
choices: Compile frontend assets
Distribute incoming traffic across multiple backends and usually avoid unhealthy ones
Convert SQL queries into NoSQL documents
Issue TLS certificates only
quiz.explanation: It spreads load and, with health checks, can take failing instances out of rotation.

quiz.question: Why can a single load balancer still be a problem?
choices: Because load balancers cannot use TCP
Because it can become a single point of failure if it is the only entry point and it goes down
Because it prevents you from using DNS
Because it makes caching illegal
quiz.explanation: Production setups often use more than one load balancer, or a managed service with redundancy.

exercise.prompt: List two load-balancing algorithms and one situation where you would pick each. Then add a note about what a health check should do if an instance starts returning 500s.
exercise.hint: Round robin is simple when instances are similar. Least connections can help if some requests are long-lived. A health check should take the failing instance out of the pool until it recovers.

lessons.title: Sharding, replication, ACID, and scaling

chapters.title: Databases (Sharding, Replication, ACID, Vertical & Horizontal Scaling)

lessons.summary: The course treats a database deep-dive as essential for system design interviews. Vertical scaling means a bigger machine; horizontal scaling means more machines. Replication copies data to other nodes for reads, backups, or failover. Sharding splits data across nodes so each holds only a part of the set. ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) describes the guarantees people expect from a transactional database, each with trade-offs in complexity, consistency, and cost.

quiz.question: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling for a database?
choices: Vertical means a larger machine; horizontal means adding more machines
Vertical means more regions only; horizontal means faster disks only
They are two words for sharding
Horizontal scaling never requires application changes
quiz.explanation: Vertical scaling is simpler until you hit the limits of one box. Horizontal scaling adds capacity by distributing work.

quiz.question: What does sharding do?
choices: It encrypts every query
It splits data across multiple nodes so each one stores only a subset
It always makes every replica identical and writable
It replaces the need for backups
quiz.explanation: A shard key decides which node owns a row or document. That is different from replication, which copies the same data.

quiz.question: What do the letters in ACID stand for?
choices: Availability, Caching, Indexing, Deployment
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Auth, Compression, I/O, Disk
Append, Copy, Import, Delete
quiz.explanation: Those four properties describe a traditional transactional store: a unit of work either completes fully, leaves valid state, does not interfere badly with others, and survives a crash once committed.

exercise.prompt: You have a users table that no longer fits on one machine. In a short paragraph, say whether you would first try vertical scaling, read replicas, or sharding, and what trade-off your first choice accepts.
exercise.hint: A common path is: bigger machine first (simple, finite), then read replicas if the bottleneck is reads (writes still hit the primary), then sharding when a single primary cannot hold or write the data (more operational complexity).
